reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: The end stage of an uncorrected large left-to-right shunt, in which pulmonary vascular disease raises pulmonary pressures until the shunt reverses and becomes right-to-left
Reversal of the shunt causes chronic hypoxaemia, central cyanosis, and secondary erythrocytosis
Common underlying defects include large ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defects, and patent ductus arteriosus
Examination shows cyanosis, clubbing, and signs of pulmonary hypertension such as a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound
Secondary erythrocytosis raises hyperviscosity concerns, but iron deficiency and paradoxical thromboembolism must also be considered
Multisystem complications include haemoptysis, arrhythmias, gout, cholelithiasis, and cerebral abscess or stroke from paradoxical emboli

Management is largely supportive and directed at complications, with pulmonary vasodilator therapy for selected patients; the underlying defect is generally no longer operable once fixed pulmonary vascular disease has developed
Pregnancy carries very high maternal and fetal mortality and is strongly discouraged
reference.pathophysiology: A large systemic-to-pulmonary shunt exposes the pulmonary circulation to high flow and pressure, driving progressive remodelling and obliteration of the pulmonary arterioles. As pulmonary vascular resistance rises and becomes fixed, pressures approach or exceed systemic levels and the shunt reverses to right-to-left. Deoxygenated blood then bypasses the lungs, causing hypoxaemia and cyanosis, which stimulates erythropoiesis and secondary erythrocytosis. The chronically pressure-loaded right ventricle eventually fails, and loss of the normal filtering of venous emboli allows paradoxical embolism to the systemic circulation.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary hypertension from chronic lung disease or thromboembolic disease
Cyanotic congenital heart disease without pulmonary vascular disease
Right heart failure of other aetiology
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to identify the underlying shunt, estimate pulmonary pressures, and assess right ventricular function
Pulse oximetry, including differential saturations where relevant
Full blood count for erythrocytosis and assessment of iron status
Right heart catheterisation to measure pulmonary pressures and resistance and test reversibility
ECG for right ventricular hypertrophy and arrhythmia
Assessment for complications such as hyperuricaemia and gallstones
redFlags: Worsening hypoxaemia or syncope indicating decompensation
Massive haemoptysis from pulmonary vascular disease
Signs of paradoxical embolism, stroke, or cerebral abscess
Sustained arrhythmia or progressive right heart failure
Pregnancy, which markedly increases the risk of death
reference.prognosis: Once fixed pulmonary vascular disease develops, the defect is usually inoperable and the condition is progressive, though many patients survive into adulthood with careful supportive care. Prognosis is limited by right heart failure, arrhythmia, haemoptysis, and thromboembolic and infective complications; targeted pulmonary vasodilator therapy has improved symptoms and outcomes for some patients.
pitfalls: Performing inappropriate venesection for erythrocytosis and precipitating iron deficiency and hyperviscosity
Overlooking iron deficiency, which worsens symptoms despite a high haematocrit
Referring for defect closure after pulmonary vascular disease has become fixed
Failing to prevent paradoxical embolism with meticulous line and air precautions
Not counselling firmly against pregnancy and about contraception
